title: Wood dust and formaldehyde: health effects and exposure limits
audience: Timber floor restoration workers and the supervisors who plan dust controls.
learningOutcomes: Describe the health effects of wood dust and formaldehyde from engineered boards.
State the exposure values quoted for wood dust and formaldehyde, and say where each value comes from.
Explain why meeting an exposure limit does not replace the control hierarchy.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: WorkSafe Victoria, Wood dust: health hazards and control (reviewed 17/04/2026); Safe Work Australia, Workplace exposure limits for airborne contaminants (April 2024; document cover); Safe Work Australia, New workplace exposure limits take effect 1 December 2026 (no date shown).

instruction.heading: What wood dust does to the body
instruction.body: WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 17/04/2026) names occupational asthma and nasal cancer among the lung diseases linked to inhaled wood dust. The same page lists nasal and eye irritation, nosebleeds, skin dermatitis and reduced lung function as effects of exposure. It also reports that the International Agency for Research on Cancer classes wood dust as carcinogenic to humans, with links to cancers of the nose, sinuses and upper throat.

instruction.heading: Formaldehyde from engineered boards
instruction.body: WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 17/04/2026) places formaldehyde in reconstituted wood products such as plywood, particleboard and fibreboard including MDF. The same page describes short-term irritation of the eyes, nose and throat, and treats formaldehyde as carcinogenic under the GHS classification that Safe Work Australia adopts. Treat sanding dust from engineered boards as a formaldehyde source as well as a wood dust source until the product information says otherwise.

instruction.heading: Exposure values and what to check
instruction.body: WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 17/04/2026) quotes, from Safe Work Australia's April 2024 list, softwood dust at 5 mg/m3 averaged over eight hours and 10 mg/m3 short-term, and certain hardwoods such as beech and oak at 1 mg/m3 averaged over eight hours. Formaldehyde is 1 ppm (1.2 mg/m3) averaged over eight hours and 2 ppm (2.5 mg/m3) short-term in that list. The formaldehyde values are confirmed in the April 2024 Safe Work Australia list.

instruction.heading: The December 2026 change
instruction.body: Safe Work Australia's news page (no date shown) says the new Workplace exposure limits (WEL) take effect on 1 December 2026, replacing the workplace exposure standards list, and that the transition period ends on 30 November 2026. The same page gives no wood dust value, and says formaldehyde is among nine substances where ministers asked for more impact analysis before its limit is updated. Check the current list on the day of the job and record the check.

instruction.heading: A limit is not permission
instruction.body: An exposure limit is a reference point for checking control. It does not make an uncontrolled sanding process acceptable. The control hierarchy is applied first, and exposure is checked against the limit to confirm the controls are working. A job that is below a limit on one day can exceed it with a different machine, a closed room or a longer shift.

procedure: Identify the timber type where known, and whether the floor uses engineered board or MDF-based material.
Apply the control hierarchy before sanding: eliminate or reduce the dust where possible, isolate, use engineering controls, then add PPE as the last layer.
Confirm the exposure limit in force on the day of the work, and record the check and its date.
Do not rely on a respirator as the main control.
Record the dust control plan and the exposure assessment before work starts.
Review the plan if the floor type, room, machine or shift length changes.

workedExamples.situation: You are asked to sand a floor laid with engineered boards that have an MDF-style core, in a small study with a closed door. The client says the boards are 'probably oak'.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which controls come first, and what do you record about the limits?
workedExamples.reasoning: Treat the dust as both wood dust and formaldehyde. Set up extraction at the machine and ventilation of the room before sanding, keep occupants out of the room, and use the approved respirator only for the risk that remains. Use the lower applicable limit until the species is confirmed, and record the check against the current list.

equipmentAndPpe: On-tool extraction and a dust collector (see “Dust control: extraction, wet cleaning and safe clean-up”)
Respiratory protection selected under the assessment (see “Respiratory protection and fit: the last layer of control”)
Current Safe Work Australia exposure limit list, with the date checked

commonErrors.error: Treating an exposure limit as a safe level for uncontrolled dust.
commonErrors.prevention: Apply the control hierarchy first, then check exposure against the limit.

commonErrors.error: Using the softwood limit for a timber that has not been identified.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the species as unidentified, and use the more conservative value until it is identified.

commonErrors.error: Assuming the April 2024 values still apply after 1 December 2026.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the list current on the day of the job and record the date.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: WorkSafe Victoria (page reviewed 17/04/2026) links inhaled wood dust to occupational asthma and nasal cancer, and reports the IARC classification of wood dust as carcinogenic to humans.
Formaldehyde limits of 1 ppm as an 8-hour average and 2 ppm as a short-term limit are confirmed in the Safe Work Australia list dated April 2024.
Partly checked: WorkSafe Victoria quotes the wood dust values from the April 2024 list, but the primary list text retrieved had no wood dust rows.
Learning these values does not grant any licence or authority to carry out regulated work.

qualityStandard: A hazard and exposure record is completed before work starts.
Controls are applied in hierarchy order and recorded.
The exposure limit check is dated and recorded.
documentationEvidence: Dust control plan for the job
Exposure limit reference used, with the date it was checked
Record of the species and board core, marked unidentified where not identified.
summary: Wood dust causes lung disease and cancer risk, and formaldehyde can come from engineered boards.
Apply the control hierarchy before relying on any limit or respirator.
Check the exposure limit that applies on the day, because the WEL change takes effect on 1 December 2026.
referencesAtEnd: Official sources to recheck before any job: WorkSafe Victoria, Wood dust: health hazards and control (reviewed 17/04/2026); Safe Work Australia, Workplace exposure limits for airborne contaminants (April 2024; document cover); Safe Work Australia, New workplace exposure limits take effect 1 December 2026 (no date shown).

knowledgeChecks.question: Which health effect does WorkSafe Victoria name for inhaled wood dust?
options: Improved lung function overall
Skin hardening only on the hands
No health effects at low levels
Occupational asthma and nasal cancer

knowledgeChecks.question: Which exposure limit is quoted for softwood dust as an 8-hour average?
options: 5 mg/m3
10 mg/m3
1 mg/m3
2 ppm

knowledgeChecks.question: From which date do the Workplace exposure limits (WEL) take effect, replacing the current exposure standards?
options: 1 January 2026
1 December 2026
30 November 2026
1 July 2024

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about the control hierarchy is correct?
options: Respirators come first on every job site and in every room at all
A low exposure limit removes the need for any controls at all
Eliminate or isolate, and use engineering controls, before relying on PPE
A dust bag on a tool is sufficient for the whole job site today

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker says the job is fine because dust is below the exposure limit. What is the correct response?
options: Agree and skip extraction, since the dust reading is low today
Ask for the limit to be ignored on this job and the next few jobs
Use compressed air to clear the dust from the floor and the walls
Still apply the controls in order, and record the exposure check
